pages.x: In the spring of 1918 a new kind of flu appeared among soldiers; one of the first known outbreaks was at an army camp in Kansas. Troopships and crowded camps carried it around the world. Spain, neutral in the war, let its newspapers report it freely, so others called it the Spanish flu.

In the autumn a far deadlier wave struck. Unlike most flu, it killed healthy young adults, often within days: their lungs filled with fluid and their faces turned blue. In October 1918 alone some 195,000 Americans died. Coffins ran short, and cities dug mass graves.

With no vaccine and no antibiotics, towns closed schools, theatres and churches, banned spitting and told people to wear gauze masks. Philadelphia went ahead with a huge parade in September, and within weeks thousands of its people were dead; St Louis closed down early and suffered far less.

The flu reached almost everywhere, from Arctic villages to Pacific islands. India suffered worst, with perhaps 12 million dead, and Western Samoa lost about a fifth of its people. In all, about a third of the people in the world caught it.

Among those who caught it and lived were the young Walt Disney, and President Woodrow Wilson, who fell ill at the peace talks in Paris in 1919. Others were not so lucky: the Austrian painter Egon Schiele died three days after his pregnant wife.
In 2005 scientists rebuilt the 1918 virus from its genes, found in preserved lung tissue and in a victim buried in the frozen ground of Alaska.
pages.fx: It turned out to be a bird flu of the kind called H1N1, and studying it helps the world prepare for the next pandemic.

pages.x: The flu of 1918 killed more people than the First World War, yet for decades it was half forgotten, buried under the memory of the war. Its lessons about masks, closing crowded places and how fast a new virus can spread came back to the world in 2020.
